title: The right to strike and BMS's approach
author: Editorial Desk
summary: BMS has joined strikes and has stayed out of others. What guides the decision.
body:
A strike is the oldest tool that workers have. When a group of workers stops work together, an employer feels the cost at once, and that is why the strike has always been the source of a union's bargaining strength. It is also why the law regulates it, why governments and courts have debated it, and why unions differ on when to use it. With a general strike called by several central trade unions for 12 February 2026, the question is in the news. This post sets out the legal position, then explains the approach that BMS has followed, and then the other view, so that readers can judge for themselves.

## Where the right to strike stands in law

India's Constitution guarantees citizens the right to form associations or unions under Article 19(1)(c). The Supreme Court has held, in T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu in 2003, that employees have no fundamental right to strike. The right is a legal right, and it exists to the extent that statutes allow, and is subject to reasonable restrictions. The ILO's conventions and supervisory bodies, on the other hand, are generally understood to recognise the right to strike as part of freedom of association, and India is a founder member of the ILO. The result is a position that unions and employers read in different ways: a legal right that the law recognises, but one that is not placed beyond regulation.

Legal history is also relevant. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 first gave limited protection to registered unions for acts done in trade disputes, and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 later set out procedures for strikes in industrial disputes. Courts have also made a distinction between a strike by workers in private industry and a strike by government employees, which is often restricted by service conduct rules.

## What the Industrial Relations Code provides

The Industrial Relations Code, which came into force with the other Labour Codes on 21 November 2025, has taken over the Industrial Disputes Act. According to the analysis by PRS Legislative Research of the Code as introduced, the main rules on strikes are these:

- Every person must give 14 days' prior notice before a strike or lock-out, and the notice is valid for up to 60 days.
- A copy of the notice must reach the conciliation officer within five days.
- A strike is barred while conciliation proceedings are on and for seven days after they end.
- A strike is also barred while proceedings before a tribunal are on and for 60 days after they end.
- These notice rules apply to all establishments. Earlier, a notice requirement applied mainly to public utility services, and PRS observed that the reason for extending it to all establishments was not clear.

For workers, the rules mean that a strike is lawful only if the steps are followed. A strike without notice, or during conciliation, may be treated as illegal, with consequences for wages and discipline. Whether these rules strike the right balance is one of the main points of dispute between unions and the Government, and some unions have criticised the extension of the notice rule to all establishments. BMS has said that it has concerns about certain provisions of the Industrial Relations Code, though it has welcomed the Codes on Wages and Social Security.

## The BMS approach: dialogue first

BMS has often said that its method is dialogue first, agitation when necessary. In practice, it uses memoranda, meetings with ministers, representations, dharnas and demonstrations. It may join a strike when it believes that the demands are genuine and when the call is not driven by party politics. It has also kept away from strikes that it regarded as political. The slogan of its founder, Dattopant Thengadi, is often quoted to explain the underlying philosophy: to nationalise the labour, to "labourise" the industry and to industrialise the nation. Behind it is the view that workers, industry and the nation are not opposed to each other, and that a union should not treat the employer or the country as an enemy.

This does not mean that BMS has never struck. Accounts of its history record that it took part in the all-India general strike of 1974, linked to the movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan, and that it joined trade union protests against changes in labour laws in 2014. In June 2020 it called a nationwide movement against privatisation of public sector undertakings. On the other hand, it declined to join the Bharat Bandh called on 20 May 2025 over the Labour Codes, calling it politically motivated, and it has now stated that it will not take part in the strike on 12 February 2026.

## The questions that BMS asks

BMS's position can be summed up in three questions it asks before joining any action:

- Is the demand about workers' interest, or about a party's agenda?
- Has the Government been given a chance to respond through talks?
- Will the action protect production and the nation's interest?

The third question reflects the philosophy: production is the source of both wages and national income, and so a strike that damages it needs a strong reason. A fair way to describe the approach is that a strike is a last resort and not a first move. In its statement of 31 January 2026, BMS said that it supports constructive and pro-labour initiatives of the Government and will continue to object to measures it considers harmful to workers.

## The other view

Other unions argue that the right to strike is the main source of workers' bargaining power, and that without a credible threat of stoppage, talks do not lead anywhere. They point to the history of labour rights, from the eight-hour day to bonus and minimum wages, many of which were won after sustained agitation. They also argue that in the present situation, with new Codes that they say tilt the balance towards employers, the right needs to be used more and not less. Many of these unions say that notice rules and long conciliation periods make a lawful strike harder to organise. The Government and BMS, on the other hand, say that the Codes contain benefits for workers and that corrections should be sought through consultation.

Both positions come from long experience, and it is a mistake to treat either as simply right or wrong. A union that strikes too easily may lose public sympathy and wages for its members, while a union that never strikes may find that its demands are not taken seriously. The practical judgement lies in the timing and the cause.

## What a worker should know

- Check whether the establishment and the dispute fall under the Industrial Relations Code and whether a notice has been given.
- Do not take part in a strike during conciliation or tribunal proceedings without legal advice on the consequences.
- Keep records of attendance and wages, because disputes about deductions for strike days are common.
- Government employees are usually governed by conduct rules that restrict strikes, and courts have supported such restrictions.

## A closing thought

A worker's right to be heard is wider than the right to strike. It includes the right to organise, to bargain, to petition and to be consulted before laws are made, such as through the Indian Labour Conference, which BMS has asked the Government to convene since it has not met since 2016. Strikes are one means of being heard, and dialogue is another. What matters most is that the worker's right is respected in either case, and that no one is forced to choose between a livelihood and a voice.
